newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey must wait till dust settles for Iraq oil.
newsitem.headline: Turkey must wait till dust settles for Iraq oil.

text.p: Turkey had pinned big hopes on revived trade with Iraq under a U.N. oil-for-food plan but must now wait until the dust settles from Tuesday's U.S. missile attacks on Iraq before the oil can flow through its pipeline.
"I don't want to use the term 'disappointed' but we now have to wait until things settle down in the region," said a senior oil official, who declined to be identified.
"We were used to waiting for the pipeline to be reopened. We have already been waiting for that for more than six years," he told Reuters.

After ordering missile attacks on targets in southern Iraq earlier on Tuesday on the grounds Iraq was attacking the Kurds in its north, U.S. President Bill Clinton said the U.N. plan to allow Iraq to sell oil to buy humanitarian supplies could not proceed under the current ciscumstances.
"Our previous expectations (for the reopening of the pipeline) had been dashed four times since the pipeline was closed in 1990," the Turkish official said.
Under the U.N. deal, signed by Iraq in May, Baghdad would be allowed $2 billion of oil sales renewable every six months, worth about 550,000 barrels per day (bpd) at last week's prices.

Most of the oil would have to be exported through the 986-km (616-mile) trans-Turkish pipeline which extends from Iraq's Kirkuk oilfields, outside the no-fly zone set above the 36th parallel in Iraq, to Turkey's Ceyhan oil terminal.

Another Turkish energy official said the latest Iraqi crisis would not affect Ankara's $23-billion natural gas deal with its eastern neighbour Iran, which allegedly sided with a rival Iraqi Kurdish group against Baghdad forces in the latest incidents.
"The Iranian deal is a distinct project. Why should it be affected by the U.S.-Iraqi friction?" he said.

Oil analysts in London said the latest military developments in northern Iraq were likely to derail the U.N. plan for limited oil sales for Iraq beyond the end of the year. They were expecting the sales to begin in September.
"Another factor that will determine the future of the region is the U.S. elections in November," said a Turkish official.

But the oil-for-food exchange was suspended by the United Nations on Sunday because of fears for the safety of aid distribution monitors following Baghdad's military incursion into northern Iraqi Kurdistan on Saturday.

Turkey said on Monday shortly before the U.S. attack that it was expecting a delay in the Iraqi oil sales, and planned to appeal to the United Nations to reverse its decision of putting the deal on hold.

Edward Gnehm, the U.S. envoy to the United Nations, said on Tuesday the terms of the memorandum of understanding signed on May 20 with Iraq for the oil-for-food sales needed to be reopened as the conditions then did not exist any more.
The state-controlled Anatolian news agency quoted government officials as saying that Turkey would ask the United States to "compensate for losses incurred due to the shut pipeline."
Turkish food and medicine suppliers have sent several missions to Iraq since June to win the lion's share of Iraq's food and medicine purchases, to be worth about $1.3 billion under the U.N. deal.
Turkey's state oil refiner Tupras had earlier asked the Iraqi government to buy 2.1 million tonnes of Iraqi oil under the U.N. plan.

Turkish traders in the southeast said they would stage a rally against the U.N. embargo on Iraq, in place since its invasion of Kuwait in 1990. Iraq was Turkey's top oil supplier and third largest trade partner before the Gulf crisis in 1990.
The United Nations has made clear that the humanitarian oil sale deal, designed to relieve suffering among the Iraqi people, should not be directly linked to Saddam's latest intervention.
Nevertheless, oil analysts said they felt the U.N. was unlikely to take any risks with the safety of dozens of aid distribution and oil sale monitors.
